article.title: Living with artificial intelligence

items.sentence_raw: This has been the decade of AI, with one astonishing feat after another.
A chessplaying AI that can defeat not only all human chess players, but also all previous human-programmed chess machines, after learning the game in just four hours?
That's yesterday's news, what's next?
True, these prodigious accomplishments are all in so called narrow AI, where machines perform highly specialised tasks.
items.explain: Q14: The passage says AI's amazing achievements are in **'narrow AI'** — machines doing *'highly specialised tasks'*. But then it says experts believe this *'restriction is very temporary'*. **'Temporary'** means it will not last — so the **future** will likely see no limits on AI. This matches option **C**: *'The future is unlikely to see limitations on the capabilities of AI'*. ***Option A is a trap*** — the passage does not say prediction is difficult, it says the limit is temporary.

items.sentence_raw: But many experts believe this restriction is very temporary.

items.sentence_raw: By mid-century, we may have artificial general intelligence (AGI) - machines that can achieve human-level performance on the full range of tasks that we ourselves can tackle.
If so, there's little reason to think it will stop there.
Machines will be free of many of the physical constraints on human intelligence.
items.explain: Q15: The passage lists human physical limits — our brains are *'slow'* and *'restricted by the dimensions of the human birth canal'*. Then it says machines will be *'free of many of the physical constraints'*. This explains **why** machines will be better — they don't have our body's limits. So the writer is **explaining why machines will be able to outperform humans**, which is option **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Our brains run at slow biochemical processing speeds on the power of a light bulb, and their size is restricted by the dimensions of the human birth canal.
items.explain: Q15: The passage lists human physical limits — our brains are *'slow'* and *'restricted by the dimensions of the human birth canal'*. Then it says machines will be *'free of many of the physical constraints'*. This explains **why** machines will be better — they don't have our body's limits. So the writer is **explaining why machines will be able to outperform humans**, which is option **A**.

items.sentence_raw: It is remarkable what they accomplish, given these handicaps.
But they may be as far from the physical limits of thought as our eyes are from the incredibly powerful Webb Space Telescope.
Once machines are better than us at designing even smarter machines, progress towards these limits could accelerate.
What would this mean for us?
Could we ensure a safe and worthwhile coexistence with such machines?
On the plus side, AI is already useful and profitable for many things, and super AI might be expected to be super useful, and super profitable.
But the more powerful AI becomes, the more important it will be to specify its goals with great care.

Folklore is full of tales of people who ask for the wrong thing, with disastrous consequences - King Midas, for example, might have wished that everything he touched turned to gold, but didn't really intend this to apply to his breakfast.
items.explain: Q16: The passage tells the King Midas story — he wished for gold but *'didn't really intend this to apply to his breakfast'*. This is an example of asking for the *'wrong thing, with disastrous consequences'*. So the story shows that **poorly defined objectives can go wrong**, which is option **B**. The key idea is that the goal was not clear enough.

items.sentence_raw: So we need to create powerful AI machines that are 'human-friendly' - that have goals reliably aligned with our own values.
items.explain: Q17: The passage says we need AI that is **'human-friendly'** with goals like ours. But the challenge is that *'we are far from reliably human-friendly ourselves'* — we do terrible things. So the difficulty is making AI **more human-friendly than we are**, which is option **D**. ***Option A is a trap*** — the problem is not encouraging humans, but making AI better than us.

items.sentence_raw: One thing that makes this task difficult is that we are far from reliably human-friendly ourselves.
items.explain: Q17: The passage says we need AI that is **'human-friendly'** with goals like ours. But the challenge is that *'we are far from reliably human-friendly ourselves'* — we do terrible things. So the difficulty is making AI **more human-friendly than we are**, which is option **D**. ***Option A is a trap*** — the problem is not encouraging humans, but making AI better than us.

items.sentence_raw: We do many terrible things to each other and to many other creatures with whom we share the planet.
If superintelligent machines don't do a lot better than us, we'll be in deep trouble.
We'll have powerful new intelligence amplifying the dark sides of our own fallible natures.
For safety's sake, then, we want the machines to be ethically as well as cognitively superhuman.
items.explain: Q18: The passage says we want machines to be *'ethically as well as cognitively superhuman'* — better than us in morals and thinking. It adds they'll be *'better than us at finding'* the moral high ground. So the writer suggests machines will be **superior to humans in certain respects**, which is option **C**.

items.sentence_raw: We want them to aim for the moral high ground, not for the troughs in which many of us spend some of our time.
Luckily they'll be smart enough for the job.
If there are routes to the moral high ground, they'll be better than us at finding them, and steering us in the right direction.
items.explain: Q18: The passage says we want machines to be *'ethically as well as cognitively superhuman'* — better than us in morals and thinking. It adds they'll be *'better than us at finding'* the moral high ground. So the writer suggests machines will be **superior to humans in certain respects**, which is option **C**.

items.sentence_raw: However, there are two big problems with this utopian vision.
One is how we get the machines started on the journey, the other is what it would mean to reach this destination.

The 'getting started' problem is that we need to tell the machines what they're looking for with sufficient clarity that we can be confident they will find it - whatever 'it' actually turns out to be.
items.explain: Q19: The passage explains the *'getting started'* problem — we must tell machines goals clearly, but this *'won't be easy'* because we are *'tribal creatures and conflicted'*. Our own **human shortcomings** make the task hard. This matches option **D**: *'Human shortcomings will make creating the machines we need more difficult'*.

items.sentence_raw: This won't be easy, given that we are tribal creatures and conflicted about the ideals ourselves.
items.explain: Q19: The passage explains the *'getting started'* problem — we must tell machines goals clearly, but this *'won't be easy'* because we are *'tribal creatures and conflicted'*. Our own **human shortcomings** make the task hard. This matches option **D**: *'Human shortcomings will make creating the machines we need more difficult'*.

items.sentence_raw: We often ignore the suffering of strangers, and even contribute to it, at least indirectly.
How then, do we point machines in the direction of something better?
As for the 'destination' problem, we might, by putting ourselves in the hands of these moral guides and gatekeepers, be sacrificing our own autonomy - an important part of what makes us human.
Machines who are better than us at sticking to the moral high ground may be expected to discourage some of the lapses we presently take for granted.
We might lose our freedom to discriminate in favour of our own communities, for example.
items.explain: Q20: The passage says we *'might lose our freedom to discriminate in favour of our own communities'*. **'Discriminate in favour of'** means **'promote the interests of'** — it's the same idea. So machines may prevent us from promoting our community's interests. The answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Loss of freedom to behave badly isn't always a bad thing, of course: denying ourselves the freedom to put children to work in factories, or to smoke in restaurants are signs of progress.
But are we ready for ethical silicon police limiting our options?
They might be so good at doing it that we won't notice them; but few of us are likely to welcome such a future.
items.explain: Q22: The passage says *'few of us are likely to welcome such a future'* with machines limiting our freedom. **'Few'** means almost no one — so most people are **not** comfortable. The question says *'Many people are comfortable'* — this is the opposite. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: These issues might seem far-fetched, but they are to some extent already here.
AI already has some input into how resources are used in our National Health Service (NHS) here in the UK, for example.
items.explain: Q24: The passage says AI already has input into how *'resources are used in our National Health Service'*. **'Resources'** means things like money, staff, and equipment — the same as **'available resources'** in the list. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: If it was given a greater role, it might do so much more efficiently than humans can manage, and act in the interests of taxpayers and those who use the health system.
However, we'd be depriving some humans (e.g. senior doctors) of the control they presently enjoy.
items.explain:
Q25: The passage says a bigger AI role would deprive *'some humans (e.g. senior doctors) of the control they presently enjoy'*. **'Senior doctors'** are **'medical practitioners'**. So certain medical practitioners would lose control. The answer is **A**.

Q26: The same sentence says senior doctors would lose *'the control they presently enjoy'*. **'Control'** here means their power to make decisions — their **'professional authority'**. So they would not have their current level of professional authority. The answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: Since we'd want to ensure that people are treated equally and that policies are fair, the goals of AI would need to be specified correctly.
We have a new powerful technology to deal with - itself, literally, a new way of thinking.
For our own safety, we need to point these new thinkers in the right direction, and get them to act well for us.
It is not yet clear whether this is possible, but if it is, it will require a cooperative spirit, and a willingness to set aside self-interest.
items.explain: Q23: The passage says achieving safety with AI *'will require a cooperative spirit, and a willingness to set aside self-interest'*. **'Cooperative spirit'** means **'work together'** — it's the same idea. So we all need to work together for machines to act in our best interests. The answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Both general intelligence and moral reasoning are often thought to be uniquely human capacities.
But safety seems to require that we think of them as a package: if we are to give general intelligence to machines, we'll need to give them moral authority, too.
And where exactly would that leave human beings?
All the more reason to think about the destination now, and to be careful about what we wish for.

subtitles: Powerful artificial intelligence (AI) needs to be reliably aligned with human values, but does this mean AI will eventually have to police those values?

orphan_explain_map.21: Q21: The passage mentions **'silicon police'** limiting our options, but it never says anything about how many would be needed. The question asks if they would need to exist *'in large numbers'* — this specific detail about quantity is completely missing. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
